item.dc:creator: Paul Sellers
item.content:encoded:
...and my, does this design of mine deliver punchy simplicity in making the simplest router plane you'll ever make!

My smallest homemade, handmade user-router plane came from a worn-out, worn-down, overused flat file I kept in a worn file box for the day when I needed tool steel for whatever and then the scrap bin of bits of wood. The brass wear plate is not really necessary, in the sense of an essential, as the wood can always be replaced for free if it does wear, but that would take a lifetime, and the plane remade from scraps is free and easy anyway. But I like the idea and the thinness of the extended front edge extension. The spalted beech is an ideal wood of free character, but any wood, even a softwood stud, will work anyway.

This is an ultra-pleasant plane to make and have ready to use; inside an hour or so, I'm almost together with it, but now I have designed and made so many router planes, 30 or more at least; I know exactly where I am going point on point. I downsized the components and used my making methods from the original instructionals we did to pass on to others via my YouTube channel and my blog here.

I know that you can make router planes smaller than this, but, really, why would you? Such smallness gives no value and meets no necessity for 99.9% of furniture-making needs. A narrow-bladed plane like this, 3-4 mm (1/8" - 3/16") offers the most minimal of resistance in the cut.

I lowered the bed angle (the slope the cutting iron sits at in the plane body) to 44 -45º+- from my original 52º in my original router plane to see what it felt like on so narrow a width of cutting iron. That was just to simplify the angles so I could use a combination square's existing 45º. The steeper angle works well on regular router planes, so I won't change that. With this downsized version, you can barely feel the shavings lifting off as long as you don't take too deep a cut.

Heating the file with a blowtorch to bright orange and leaving it to cool until handleable means you can cut the steel with a hacksaw as easily as mild steel and then file it with a hand file. No need for a mechanical grinder at all. I like to leave evidence of the original tool steel source in the metals used so file teeth, though filed down to evenness, are self-evident. 95% of all the cuts in the steel, the bevel, the notches, etc., came from the hacksaw and were finessed with a flat file. A final rub with wet and dry -400 left the steel feeling soft and pleasant. Aesthetically, the final look I wanted is achieved.

The 1.5 mm brass plate cuts easily with both hacksaw and file. There will be some conflict between the wood's exchanges of moisture levels and the brass remaining true to the original cut size.

I used contact cement to maximise adhesion quality. This will never turn loose, but I also added extra belts and braces by using some screws through the plate.

The hanger bolts are common enough hardware available online via eBay and Amazon, as are the 4mm (M4 by 10mm) by 10mm knurled high-type thumb nuts. Three of the 4mm by 40mm hanger bolts and thumb nuts, plus two 4mm split washers and four 4mm washers takes care of what you buy in as hardware.

The spring or split washer between two ordinary 4mm washers allows mechanical pressure to be applied to the retainer bar, which spans the blade in situ. Instead of cinching both nuts tight, cinch them tight and then turn back a single turn. This then gives enough pressure to keep the cutting iron hard down while at the same time allows for any further adjustment without having to tighten and slacken the retainer bar nuts.

The simplicity of making this hand router plane is the single piece of wood and the two scallops each side where the thumbs provide the push points in using the plane rather than attaching knobs.

The slight discrepancy between wood and brass wear place is of no material consequence, but consider making the brass plate 1 mm undersize, and it will never show.

The retainer bar is 68 mm (2 1/2") long by 20 mm (3/4") wide and 3 mm (1/8") thick.

The two 4 mm holes in the retainer bar are bored on 50 mm (2") centres.

The blade recess is a millimeter less than the thickness of the blade, so pressure on the back of the blade from the retainer bar holds the blade firmly to depth.

If you like the idea of measured increment marks, measure the teeth of the file. Often, as in my case here, the teeth will be at metric increments. I know that it seems odd, but I live in both imperial and metric measuring and use both all the time and at the same time. Measuring my half inch and dividing the number of teeth showed that a single full revolution deepened the cut by a fraction I could relate to my work. Because the bed angle is near enough 45º, a full revolution of the depth adjuster deepened the pass by a fixed amount, and I could set the depth according to the teeth on the file. A full revolution deepened the cut by half a millimeter. I mark the adjuster with a Sharpie to see exactly where the turn starts and ends.

It may not be obvious, but the two notches allow for deeper housing dadoes. Also, you can flip the knurled thumb nut, which gives you from minus zero on through whatever depth you need.

You can still support our work by buying our full-size hand router plane kit which provides all the hardware here.

I will post on another couple of hand router planes I have made that you will also love to make and own soon.
